speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, debating this bill is like arguing against motherhood. There is not a single person in the House-and I do not think there are too many people in Canada-who would not be happy to do something directly, not only for the working poor- which this bill addresses-but for any of the people in Canada who are in poverty today, in fact anybody in the world who is in poverty.
A person has to consider what, in fact, is in the best interest of the working poor of Canada. Is it to continue the process of spending more than one has? Driving the national debt up? Borrowing from our children to pay for today? Or, is it in fact to establish an economic program that is sound and that will take us into the future where our children and our grandchildren can look at a country where they not only have a job but they see far reduced levels of poverty in the working poor, as well as in any other category, whether it is the seniors or the children.
Whenever a Conservative in particular stands up to address a topic like this, people immediately say: "Oh, he is a Conservative. He doesn't care about people." I would like to point just a brief example.
It is not just Canadians who think this way. There are other countries around this world which also recognize that you cannot give something out unless you have the money in pocket. To take another country in America, if you look at Mexico, it has far more people in poverty than we in Canada. If you want to call it working poor, most of those people are working and they are very poor.

What is in their best interests? Is their government's approach to try to solve that poverty without an improved economy? It has tried, but it does not work. We cannot improve the plight of the working poor without upgrading our economy. That is the task that this government has undertaken.
But, in every step of the way in trying to improve this economic condition in Canada, we have been opposed. At first I thought it was just politics, but I have come to realize that many people in the opposition actually believe in what they are saying and what they are doing. They do not believe that you need to have a sound economy before you can spend the money-

speechtext: Yes, we do.

speechtext:
-that if you want to spend more, no matter what the cause, that it is okay, that somehow or other that debt does not really count.
I do not believe that, Mr. Speaker, and thank goodness a number of people in Canada do not believe that. Just as an example, the economic program that this government has established is a sound one. We believe that if you want a bigger piece of pie, you have to get a bigger pie.
That is a simple analogy. You do not need to be a rocket scientist to figure that one out. If you want more pie, you have to have a bigger pie in total. Our policies are encouraging that. But what has happened? Just this fall we saw nearly a year's backlog of sound economic legislation being held up by our friends down the hall. The first was Bill C-21, the reform UI bill, very important to this country. If you want to upgrade the working poor, especially the ones who need to get from a low paying job to a better paying job, you need a program that is going to work on training and education. Part of that was in Bill C-21. That was one of the main reasons for it. It was a a reform UI bill that would provide some of the help that the opposition is actually looking for.
We had Bill C-28, another tax reform, to try to get greater taxation from large corporations. That was held up. We have Bill C-69, the government expenditure restraint bill, again trying to put this economy on a sound footing. That also was held up.

These, if they had not passed, would have added billions to our deficit.
Now, what is the bill currently being held up? It is the goods and services tax, a tax designed to improve our local industry, to make us more competitive on world markets, to take away the unfair competition that importers have over the producers of our own products, to try to put our exporters on an equal footing.
The bill does more than that. It adds capital initiative to the whole economy, up to $9 billion a year initiative that is in fact going to end up with a net result of more jobs and more dollars for the exact people we are talking about today.
Also, in passing, it helps businesses so that their capital and operating costs are more effective, more competitive, and of course therefore providing more jobs.
If we really want to assist the working poor, I would encourage the hon. members who proposed this bill to urge their friends down the hall to in fact pass it.
These bills are the ones we have just passed in the last year to try to improve our economy, but we have been practising economic policy for six years now. What is the result of that? It has been aimed at restraint, at tax reform, and at improving our whole economy.
Let us address restraint just briefly. In spite of the fact that 33 per cent of our government spending is for transfer of spending, there is another 24 per cent in transfers to the provinces. These are the dollars that go directly, in most cases, to the kinds of people who need it the most. It is transfers for the elderly. They get $17 billion per year. Their increases over the last five years have been at a rate exceeding 7 per cent. There are the UI recipients. There is family allowance for the young people we are talking about. There is veterans allowances. Under the transfers to the provinces, there are the hospitals, the schools and, of course, the welfare payments that are very important. All of those have been increasing at close to 6 per cent per annum. Yet, the total government spending has been at a rate of 3.6 per cent. It is obvious that we have been cutting back on many other aspects of our program. It is an example I have used in the House. I would like to repeat it one more time.
When we took office, this government was spending $10 billion per year more than it was bringing in in revenue. Currently, we are bringing in $10 billion more in a year than we are spending. That is a $26 billion a year turnaround to tiy to get this country back in shape so that we can afford the programs that we all wish we could provide for the working poor.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would ask again for the consent of the House that two Liberals could be allowed to speak in succession. In
a few days, Mr. Speaker, most Canadians will celebrate Christmas, time for culinary traditions, joy, peace, religious ceremonies, family reunions, and gift sharing. For most of them it will be a time to rejoice, yet an ever increasing number of Canadians will only be able to remember better days. What with increasing lay-offs and practically nonexisting opportunities to find alternate employment at decent wages, our population is getting poorer at an alarming rate! We are in a recession, the government promises to implement the GST next month, and chances of landing permanent jobs are getting slimmer by the minute.
Mr. Speaker, food banks, clothing distribution centres and people queuing for a bowl of soup are increasingly common. Still we lack the resources and the funds to bring a minimum of relief to the ever larger numbers of needy people.

Poverty is being felt throughout this country and some areas are touched more than others. From Vancouver's lower east side to Halifax's north end, from Winnipeg's core area to Toronto's Jane, Finch and Regent Park complexes to name but a few, poverty is fast becoming a fact of life of too many fellow Canadians.
December 10,1990

Supply

Just as an example, in one month a food bank in the Montreal region counted roughly 1,200 people, including 400 children under age 15 who were so hungry they could not wait to eat whatever they could find in the grocery bags! These children often leave for school without eating anything because there is nothing to eat at home. These children have a hard time concentrating and learning on an empty stomach.
A child with an empty stomach finds it hard to listen to what the teacher has to say.
Mr. Speaker, those children will be our next adult generation. They are the ones who will have to fashion to future of our country. And they will be our judges.
That so many children live in poverty in a society like ours is intolerable. According to the Canadian Association of Food Banks, the parents of over one million children must rely on food banks to feed their children every day.
Mr. Speaker, it also intolerable that so many young need to escape trough artificial means in order to survive in a world that has let them down. We are talking about young people who live in this very country. We are talking about our own young people. About youth who have a potential to offer, but whose essential needs are not met.
What is this government going to do about it? When will it make poverty in Canada a priority on its agenda? Poverty is not only a provincial responsibility, it is also a federal responsibility.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote Judge Ruffo who is well known for her stand for children: "Our children are trying to tell us something, but we aren't listening. Our children have no hope so they are destroying themselves in drugs and suicide and prostitution and committing more and more violent crimes".
We must all stop ignoring the problem. We must get involved. This government must admit that there is a crisis, that there is indeed an emergency. This government must get involved before it is too late. It might already be too late. Throwing the problem in another
camp will only delay things. Those in power must act now or there will not be a tomorrow for thousands of Canadian kids. When will this government commit itself? When will it accept to do something?

Mr. Speaker, whether we like it or not, the problem is here and, far from going away, it is growing, Pediatricians report that the number of cases of ear infection, pneumonia, diarrhea and meningitis among children of low-income families is increasing. Child abuse is on the rise: 36 and 35 per cent respectively among girls and boys age 14 and 15 in Canada were victims of sexual abuse. How long will this government wait before taking action? When will this government accept to face the music and realize that the problem is in its own backyard?
Mr. Speaker, poverty goes hand in hand with all the other social ills. It is urgent to find and implement ways to put an end to this critical situation.
According to Statistics Canada, one child in ten lives in poverty. The death rate among new bom babies of poor parents is twice the national average. The rate of school dropouts among children of poor families is 2.2 times higher than for other children. What a sad picture!
What will tomorrow be like if we refuse to face these facts? When will the Prime Minister make Canadian men and women a priority? In Canada, the number of poor people, among all age groups, is increasing. Unfortunately, this is a well established fact. Hardship is no longer limited to some social classes and certain age groups.
Bankrupcies plant and store closures, job losses and salary cuts are every day occurrences. Overnight, Canadian men and women by the thousand find themselves financially destitute.
How can we believe in a country which so easily neglects its own citizens? There is no longer any income security or any hope to make dreams come true. A much too large proportion of our citizens have a very uncertain future. What tragedy will have to happen before this government wakes up and implements programs in co-operation with the provinces? The situation has become unacceptable and yet, only a modicum of help is being offered. We expect voluntary agencies to do everything, but it is not possible, it is not enough.

December 10,1990

Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention the situation of our senior citizens, too quickly forgotten by a society moving in high gear. To illustrate what I want to say I will give you the example of the group Sun Youth in Montreal, which announced that it would hold, last November 21st, a distribution of used clothing for older people. It was supposed to start at 8.30 a.m., but at 6 a.m. people started to line up. More than 1,200 people over 60 came to get free clothing, and this during a single day. These are people who barely managed on their pension or welfare cheque. Once they have paid for rent and some food they have nothing left. Mr. Abramson, 74, who was in charge of the quality of clothing said and I quote: "Senior citizens are the most mistreated of our citizens. Governments have money for this or that, but nothing for those who helped build this country and paid for it with their taxes."
Mr. Speaker, what more does this government want? Our children are going to school hungry; teenagers struggle for survival in the street due to a lack of income and decent employment; our senior citizens line up to get free clothing to face the elements.
We are often told that: "Canada is a rich country, a caring country, but for who? When will the gouvemment acknowledge that this country is in a crisis, not just a recession? When will the government put in place job creation programs to offset all the closings and to increase the number of jobs available? When will the gouvemment invest in this country and give equal opportunities to all its citizens? When is the government going to act?

Mr. Speaker, I have here a document dealing with Canadian children which I received recently from Statistics Canada. By the way, I wish to congratulate Statistics Canada for providing hon. members with this very useful tool.
In this document I have found rather alarming data concerning children living below the poverty line. Here are a few facts: In 1988, 4 per cent of children lived in families where the annual income was below $10,000; 11.7 per cent lived in families where the annual income was between $10,000 and $19,999, that is to say, between $10,000 and $20,000. These two groups together represent nearly 15 per cent of the population.
What I find even more appaling, Mr. Speaker, are the following statistics: When we consider single-parent families, where the heads, in 80 per cent of the cases, are women, 23.9 per cent of children live in families where the income is below $10,000 per year, and what is even more surprising, 41.5 per cent belong to families where the income is between $10,000 and $20,000 per year. If we combine both these figures, we find the following statistics: 65.4 per cent of children from single-parent families belong to families where the income is under $20,000 a year.
I wish to in view of these disturbing figures ask my hon. friend if she does not feel that the time has come for all levels of government to make sure that former spouses-men most of the time-do their part in providing for their families after a separation or a divorce. In my opinion, these statistics are a national disgrace and I would hope that the various governments will deal with this issue and make sure than men-I say men, because these estranged spouses are almost always men-provide for their children after a marriage breakdown. May I ask my hon. friend to comment on this.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to my colleague and I am grateful to him for giving me this opportunity to speak about children that have been forgotten in the vacuum left as a result of family divorce or break-up.
For a number of years now the two government levels have been throwing the problem back and forth between themselves. They say: "Not our fault, this is a provincial responsibility. There is no federal legislation covering that aspect". I would suggest that time has come indeed for both government levels to assume their responsibilities.
I want to get back to the situation of these children, if my colleague will allow me. Earlier today the minister was telling us that the number of poor children, children who go hungry, is going down. That is quite false! On the island of Montreal the numbers are not going down.
Here is an example concerning schools. La Salle's Saint-Jean-Baptiste school ranks 70th among Montreal's poorest. If we talk about the city of Montreal it is even worse. But for the whole island the figures are dismal, 41 per cent in one school. Referring to the island or only the city of Montreal as such, we are looking at
December 10,1990

almost 40 per cent in practically every ward. The mortality rate in the poorest areas is 68 years of age, against 80 in the richest district.
One out of four Montrealers lives in poverty. These are not the figures which the minister gave us this afternoon for last year or the year before, no, these are the findings of the latest surveys made in Montreal. I think that the government has the duty to help Canadian men and women who live below the poverty level.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this very important debate. I must say, as an aside in beginning this debate, that I am a little surprised by the unwillingness of the NDP to participate in the way that we wish to participate.
It is a party that has long prided itself on cornering the market on the concern for the poor but, when a push comes to a shove, it has singularly been unable to provide speakers for this very important debate. I certainly hope it is not a sign that it puts the partisanship of a by-election, where its members are working today, over an important debate on the future of this country.

speakerposition: Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Well, they are not going to win in that by-election anyway.

Perhaps, but the people of Canada expect members to come in and debate these issue very seriously-
This has been a very good opportunity to hear different points of view on the poor of Canada. Sometimes in reciting our concerns for money, as we have heard from the government side, and some of the problems that have emerged in our economy, we lose sight of what these figures mean. What does it mean to have a reduction in funds?
Let us look at the big question of what happened in the early part of 1980s, and why a deficit was created versus what is happening right now.
In the first case, the deficit was created because the Liberal Party was too generous to the poorer regions of the country. Year after year we tried to increase the amount of moneys we gave to the provinces. People forget that. For example, from 1979-80 through to
Supply
1984-85, before this miserable government took over, we went from $1.8 billion in transfer payments to over $4 billion. That is an increase of over 100 per cent. The deficit, of course, has gone up from just over $120 billion right up to $400 billion. The government has been niggardly toward the provinces. It has increased the transfer payments by only 30 per cent.
There has been a tremendous, negative impact across the country as a result. We raise questions constantly in the House having to do with food banks. They should look at reality of 1.4 million people at various times during the year having to go to food banks and deal with the reality that by the third week of the month people are out of money.
They should deal with the reality that there is a welfare economy out there and people are pushed into lousy housing. They should deal with the reality they cannot feed and clothe their children, not make denials or say that they do not have any money. There is money in this country. They should check out the profits, the way in which people spend their money, and the charter flights to the States. They should check out their friends. There is money if we have the guts to work for the poor.
I challenge this government to work for once for the poor and not against them. The food banks have come to the Parliament of Canada, not looking for a legal argument from the Minister of Health and Welfare that it is not his responsibility. They have come with the very important desire to see that the right to eat and to have food is considered a basic human right in this country. When, since the Depression, have we had Canadians coming to this building asking to be fed as a right? We have all assumed we would feed each other. We have all assumed that volunteers could do it or that government could do it. The volunteers are tired, and the government is saying it has no money.
On this side of the House we believe that the government has a responsibility. We want the minister to step forward and begin to outline a plan of action so that Canadians can be fed, housed, and clothed.
Throughout this country it affects people from all walks of life. Nobody plans on being poor, but people do end up being poor. Let us quit blaming the victims. Let

us quit pretending that somehow people got themselves into this trap because of their own doing.
They should look at the job losses in the last month alone in Ontario and Quebec. All those ministers are sitting quietly there thinking that they do not have to worry about it because it is out there and not in their region of the country. They should check with the people at home at Christmas. This is a problem in their constituencies. This is a problem among their voters. They want to have some reassurance from this government that it understands what is going on.
I would like to talk to the House about a very important poverty problem in the city of Winnipeg. For the last 10 years, the three levels of government under the leadership originally of the member for Winnipeg South Centre brought forward a program called the core area initiative, which is perhaps the most innovative program, without exaggeration, in North America. It has been an award winning program. All three levels of government have contributed and worked hard together. They have probably generated $.5 billion in investment and expenditures in an area. Winnipeg has developed, I am very sad when I say this, into one of the poorest regions of the country. It and downtown Montreal have the most pressing urban poverty questions dealing with people who have ended up so poor that they cannot deal with that reality.
The minister of energy, who is responsible for this program on behalf of the federal government, said in the press, to the mayor of Winnipeg, and to the premier of Manitoba last week that he was not sure he could find the money. He was not sure that the program was any good. He was not sure that the accountability was appropriate. He was not sure whether he wanted to deal with the city of Winnipeg any further. He was not sure until he heard from the people of Winnipeg and therefore he wanted public hearings.
The language of public participation and public hearings is something we all generally support. We want the government to have some hearings. But what he did not say in public-and it is what every person in Winnipeg who is concerned about the future of the core will say-was that he has never shown up at public hearings. He refuses to answer correspondence. He refuses to take phone calls. He will not talk to the people until it is too late.
In downtown Winnipeg, the urban futures group headed by a very respected academic from the University of Winnipeg has just completed five months of hearings, five evenings plus private hearings. They had 95 presentations. Every major group concerned about the future of the downtown made a presentation. They were listened to and out of that came a very important report. In that report they wanted to send a message to the governments in Manitoba, at city hall and in Ottawa that the core area initiatives should be continued. They ask:
Continue the tripartite commitment to inner city revitalization. Much has been accomplished by the CAI, but much more needs to be done. The time has come to reassess direction and focus, not to abandon the undertaking and leave that which has been achieved vulnerable to erosion.
It is the absence of other programs that terrifies the people in the inner city.
We talk about refugee programs, immigration programs and the cutbacks that are hitting the new poor in this country. When we talk about cutbacks to aboriginal language programs, to aboriginal education, to aboriginal training programs, and to aboriginal economic development projects, we are talking about the same people in the core area initiative. When we talk about the lack of funding for university education, we are talking about people-

The second thing the group was looking for was to give priority to initiatives that foster community and individual empowerment and that directly improved the conditions in which current inner-city residents lived. To accomplish this, they asked that government broaden the partnership to include a much greater planning and decision-making role for inner-city communities, second, that they provide greater support to education, training, employment, community-based economic development and social service initiatives that promote ownership, self-help and self-determination, not depen-

He speaks about funding for the poor in Canada and he especially made reference to the aboriginal community. Is he aware, first of all, that the Canadian Aboriginal Economic Development Program, which is close to half a million dollars for the next five years, was increased more than inflation, close to 8 per cent year-over-year from the previous funding?
That program includes in it a whole host of self-help programs, including the small business start-up program which was increased from $72 million to $80 million a year. It is a program which is my responsibility. We were able to get that increase above 10 per cent year-overyear. Is he aware that that program has created 5,000 different, small businesses, on and off reserves, in the last five years? Is he aware that that program has done more than any previous federal government program for reducing dependency and creating entrepreneurship, creating jobs and creating business on and off the reserves, and that it has been increased far above the

level of inflation, far above almost any other line in the federal government budget?

Mr. Speaker, in a debate of honesty and sincerity, one recognizes that there are always ministers who try. But the problem becomes that, for these small efforts, they expect to be congratulated. Unemployment on the reserves remains somewhere between 80 per cent and 95 per cent. In Winnipeg there are probably somewhere in the neighbourhood of 50,000 unemployed aboriginals. Anybody who can stand up and say that this program has made a substantial difference in the community simply ignores the reality of the depth of poverty. The problem with this government is that it gets to be defensive about these issues instead of saying that it has started but it has not really accomplished anything.
The major programming that affects the plight of aboriginal people is not only the on-reserve programs such as education. Do not forget the tremendous changes created by the people returning to reserves on issues of housing. The government is probably 15 years behind in housing programs. Just when we found out last year that young people wanted to go to post-secondary education facilities more than ever before, they are faced with a government cutback. We heard in Question Period today about the need for further funds in Labrador.
We find that at the very moment in which we see a tremendous amount of pride emerging in the aboriginal community, this minister and the minister of Indian affairs, since the crisis in the summer, standing up and saying, "Don't you understand how much we have done for them".
When people have a good working relationship, they do not have to stand up and tell people how much they are doing for each other. These people understand it. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today on a point of order concerning the legislation we shall be considering later this afternoon. I spent almost all afternoon reading the legislation. I found some rather strange things and I would like to comment on them now here in the House.
I looked up Standing Order 81(5) which reads as follows, in English, and I quote:

Supplementary estimates shall be referred to a standing committee or committees immediately they are presented in the House. Each such committee shall consider and shall report, or shall be deemed to have reported, the same back to the House not later than three sitting days before the final sitting or the last allotted day in the current period.

Mr. Speaker, it is quite obvious that today is the last day of the period. It is also obvious that two standing committees of this House did not meet to consider the supplementary estimates. The two committees were the Standing Committee on Transport and the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations.
Mr. Speaker, we have evidence that this is so. On Monday, December 5, the hon. member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell said in the House that he had written a letter with three other colleagues in, the Liberal caucus to the Clerk of the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations, asking him to arrange for a meeting of the committee. However, he said that this was impossible. Obviously a committee that did not meet could not have examined estimates.
On October 18 last, the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan raised a question of privilege in the House and indicated the Standing Committee on Transport had held one meeting, but that all members of the government had stayed away from it. On November 28 last, the Speaker gave his decision on the question of privilege and said the following:

I have to say to hon. members and to the public that the working of committees is very important to the working of the House of Commons. I do ask hon. colleagues to make every effort possible to come to whatever agreements and understandings among themselves which are necessary to make these committees work.

If those committees are so important, as the Speaker said, and I agree with him, it is crucial that they meet, pursuant to the Standing Orders of the House, particularly section 81(5).

We were told when this was raised last week by the House leader for this party, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, that debate could take place in this Chamber on these estimates on the allotted days.
I have already indicated there are six allotted days in the supply period. Today is day number six. Day number five was on November 21. In other words, all five days had elapsed on November 21 before these supplementa-
December 10, 1990

ry estimates were tabled on November 23. The government apparently held back these supplementary estimates so there was only one day left in the House to discuss them, which is not in breach of the rules, and I cannot complain on that score. But for the government House leader to suggest, as he did, that somehow we had an opportunity to debate these estimates on supply days was utter nonsense because today is the only day we have an opportunity to debate them. These particular estimates in these two committees could not be considered in the committees because the committees could not meet because the government refused to allow them to meet in clear breach of the obligations under the rules.
The point that has to be made here is that on November 23 when the supplementary estimates were tabled in the House, the President of the Treasury Board, who I am sure took advice from his colleague, the Leader of the Government in the House-and clearly it was misguided advice in the circumstances-proposed a motion to refer these estimates to various committees.
The two that I think are worth noting are the references to the Standing Committee on Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Government Operations. There were a series of votes referred there and then there were three votes referred to the Standing Committee on Transport.
I have filed with the Clerk of the House a notice of objection in respect to every single one of those votes. A motion of concurrence has been proposed by the President of the Treasury Board to concur in these 17 or so votes because of these notices of objection.
My point is that the notices of objection relate to these particular items because they could not be considered in committee because the government refused absolutely to allow these committees to meet. There is ample evidence contained in the proceedings in Hansard to which I have referred on the dates that were raised by hon. members and which were not effectively refuted by any member of the government. No one stood up on the government side and said: "We have done our best to get these committees together". They, in fact, had done their best to stop these committees from meeting.
